Polarized proof nets.

These are my personal notes from the paper “Polarized proof nets and $\lambda\mu$-calculus” by Olivier Laurent. I assume an introductory knowledge of linear logic and some necessary concepts from graph theory.

Positive and negative formulas for MELL.

The formulas are given by the following grammar generated by two symbols $N$ (which corresponds to negative formulas) and $P$ (which corresponds to positive fornulas).

\[P :: = X \ \ \mid \ \ !N \otimes P\] \[N :: = X^\perp \ \ \mid \ \ ?P \times N\]

Moreover we define an involutive operation $(.)^\perp$ on formulas as follows: \(P^{\perp} =\)

Proof structures.

A proof structure is a finite directed graph with additional data, defined as follows:

  • A set of vertices.

  • A set of directed edges with the following characteristic. For a given edge $y$ there is a corresponding unique initial vertex and there could be a corresponding unique final vertex. That is vertices are allowed to not have an endpoint but are forced to have a beginning.

  • For each vertex there is a unique label in the following set of words ${ \text{ax, cut, c, w, ?d, !, \text{par}}, \otimes }$

  • For each edge there is a unique label composed of a formula and either a $+$ or $-$ sign.

  • The rules for constructing a proof structure are shown below, where the second component of the label of the edges dictates the possibility of composing these structures

What is a box?

A box is nothing less than a proof structure $\cal B$ that has as conclusions $\Gamma, N$ where $\Gamma$ is a set of input formulas and anti-output formulas and where $N$ is an input formula. This is a slight generalization from $!$ introduction rule in linear logic.

What are proof structures?.

A proof structure thus is a graph that has formulas as the labels of their edges but built in a rather naive way. That is, not every proof structure represents a formula that is valid in linear logic. The magic of the proof nets is that it suffices to check some strictly graph-theoretical properties in order to guarantee completeness with respect to linear logic.
